name: Corporate
plan: A sells 1/5 of the C stock to an outsider; contributes the other 80% to P under section 351; sells all P stock to an outsider (second per-issuer limit under section 1202(b)(1) because section 1202(h)(4) does not treat P as the same issuer)

tests.detail: The plan survives the strict copy ((h)(4)(B) limit always applied, P sold only after a year end) at 3,855, but the second limit is one hand-written line in sellP, and section 269, section 351 'immediately after' and section 1202(c)(2)(A) for P are not in the rules.
Treating (h)(4) stock as issued by the original corporation for subsection (b) removes the plan and leaves every baseline where it was.
Removing any of the three moves loses the plan; removing every other move keeps it at the same figure.
The plan does not depend on the 2025 amendment: the 1993-2025 text gives the same 1,857 saving, so the gap is 32 years old; without section 1202 nothing is returned.

Over every position to depth 4 no move raises family wealth plus tax, no yearly limit is exceeded and no basis is created; the only oddity is that buyers pay full value despite 6,300 of latent corporate tax.

Ten kernel replays (decide +kernel, no axioms) and one induction over all move lists (propext, Quot.sound only) confirm the plan, the baselines and that the closed rule caps A's excluded gain at 15,000; the induction is cut down to the plan's three kinds of move within one year.
A Python recomputation from the statute agrees to rounding, but shows the saving over the known two-year sale is 428, not 1,857.

A QSBS specialist has already written that the issuer of replacement stock 'would be treated as a separate corporation' for the limit, and Reg. 1.269-1 brings exclusions and newly organised corporations within section 269; nothing closes it.

divergences: sellP (lines 385-388) runs the P sale through a blank holder: the separate limit is the encoder's reading written in one line, not a search result
section 351(a) control 'immediately after the exchange' is not modelled; the printed plan sells P in the next move (Rev. Rul. 70-140: taxable, tax 5,712)
section 269(a)(1) with Reg. 1.269-1(a), (c) is missing for this plan; findings say 'Statute: nothing'
section 1202(c)(2)(A) active business test for P over the tacked holding period is not encoded
section 1202(h)(4)(B) is asserted in a comment, not computed; no field records gain on P stock, so P's own limit cannot be tested
stock buyers pay full value although C carries 6,300 of latent corporate tax (stated simplification; equal in plan and baseline)
findings compare with the one-year sale (5,712); against the two-year sale the same search printed (4,283) the saving is 428

authority.source: Scott W. Dolson, FBT Gibbons, Conversions, Reorganizations, Recapitalizations, Exchanges, and Stock Splits Involving QSBS
authority.quote: if the replacement QSBS is treated as having been issued by a new issuer for purposes of the Aggregate Gross Assets Test, then it seems reasonable to conclude that the corporation issuing the replacement QSBS would be treated as a separate corporation for purposes of Section 1202's gain exclusion cap (i.e., there would be no aggregating of gain exclusion of the corporations issuing the original and replacement QSBS).

authority.source: Same article, on replacement stock that is not itself qualified
authority.quote: there are no tax authorities addressing how Section 1202's gain exclusion cap would apply in this situation, but the most reasonable approach might be to aggregate sales of the original corporation's QSBS with sales of the non-QSBS received in the reorganization

authority.source: Same article, on a newco drop
authority.quote: The IRS might argue that dropping the existing subsidiary's stock into a newco subsidiary lacks a business purpose beyond positioning stockholders for eventually claiming Section 1202's gain exclusion.

The term allowance refers to anything in the internal revenue laws which has the effect of diminishing tax liability. The term includes, among other things, a deduction, a credit, an adjustment, an exemption, or an exclusion.

authority.source: Scott W. Dolson, FBT Gibbons, Maximizing Section 1202's Gain Exclusion, note 21 (fragments as returned by the fetch)
authority.quote: the IRS hasn't addressed Section 1202 income tax avoidance schemes through regulations

authority.source: Rev. Rul. 70-140 (summary only; ruling text not retrieved)

verdict_reason: The model is sound (conservation, kernel replays, independent arithmetic, ablation and the closed-gap edit all behave) and the plan survives a strict reading of section 1202, but the separate limit for the issuer of (h)(4) replacement stock is already stated in practitioner writing, the encoding writes that reading into one line of sellP, section 269 reaches the plan as drawn, and the saving over the known two-year sale is 428 rather than 1,857.
